questions.explanation: Catalogues and targeted email asking for a trackable response are classic direct marketing tools, and the order codes show its measurability. There is no live two-way conversation, so it isn't personal selling.

questions.stem: Which description best captures the strengths and weaknesses of direct marketing?
options: Highly credible but hard to control
Reaches mass audiences cheaply but gives little feedback
Changes behaviour quickly but invites price wars
Targeted and measurable, but costly and raises privacy concerns
questions.explanation: Direct marketing reaches specific individuals and its responses can be counted, but building and maintaining databases is costly and consumers worry about privacy. 'Highly credible but hard to control' describes publicity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a direct marketing tool?
questions.explanation: Direct mail, catalogues, telemarketing, direct response TV, and email are direct marketing tools that seek a response. A press release is a public relations tool aimed at earning media coverage.

questions.stem: Strata Sneakers sends promotional emails to its opted-in subscriber list. How is this classified in the course materials?
options: It is a direct marketing tool and, on the digital channels slide, paid media
It is personal selling and, on the digital channels slide, owned media
It is public relations and, on the digital channels slide, earned media
It is sales promotion and, on the digital channels slide, owned media
questions.explanation: Email is one of the direct marketing tools in the textbook, and the Keller/Swaminathan digital channels slide lists e-mail marketing under PAID media. Many students pick owned because the list belongs to the company, but the course slide classifies email marketing as paid.

questions.stem: In a hit Canadian streaming comedy, the main characters always drink Polar Peak iced tea with the label clearly visible; Polar Peak paid the producers for this exposure. This is:
questions.explanation: Paid inclusion of a brand within entertainment content is product placement. Sponsorship would mean paying to attach the brand's name to an event, team, or cause, such as a festival stage.

questions.stem: Summit Credit Union pays a fee to have its name on the Edmonton Folk Festival's main stage and its logo on all festival materials. This is:
questions.explanation: Paying a fee to be associated with someone else's event in exchange for exposure is sponsorship. Product placement puts a brand inside entertainment content such as a show or movie, not on an event stage.

questions.stem: What best distinguishes event marketing from sponsorship?
options: Event marketing builds an experience that brings consumers and the brand together; sponsorship pays a fee for association with an event, team, or cause
Event marketing is always unpaid publicity earned through news coverage; sponsorship is always paid advertising bought in mass media
Event marketing targets channel members such as retailers; sponsorship targets ultimate consumers, media, and the public
Event marketing is used only in the decline stage to clear stock; sponsorship is used only during the introduction stage
questions.explanation: Event marketing puts the brand at the centre of an experience (often one the brand creates, like a pop-up), while sponsorship buys association with an event or property someone else owns. Both are pull tools aimed at consumers in Figure 12-2, so saying event marketing targets channel members is wrong.

questions.stem: Why do marketers use product placement?
options: It guarantees the brand full control over how, when, and how often it appears on screen
It persuades retailers and wholesalers to give the brand more shelf space and feature pricing
It is required by the CRTC for any brand that also advertises on Canadian television
It shows the brand within entertainment people choose to watch, which feels less intrusive than a commercial
questions.explanation: Product placement reaches consumers inside content they've chosen to watch, so it can get past ad avoidance and feels natural. It does not guarantee control, since producers decide how the scene plays, and persuading retailers is a push objective.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of product placement?
options: A laptop brand used by the hero in a Canadian film, paid for by the maker
A car brand driven by characters in a racing video game under a paid deal
A bank's logo painted on the boards of a hockey arena it pays to sponsor
A paid soft-drink can placed on the desk of a late-night talk-show host
questions.explanation: Product placement is paid inclusion of a brand inside entertainment content. A logo on arena boards in exchange for a fee is sponsorship (signage at a sponsored venue), not placement within a show, film, or game.

questions.stem: Laila purchases groceries from FoodMart. FoodMart offers her a membership card, which entitles Laila to coupons, lucky draws, and discounts on her continued purchases at FoodMart. Which of the following tools is FoodMart using to drive the customer through the customer advocacy funnel?
questions.explanation: Customer loyalty is encouraged through CRM programs that reward continued purchases, so a membership card with coupons, draws, and discounts puts FoodMart in the loyalty stage. Engagement would involve inviting her to participate in the product experience and interact with its marketing, not rewarding repeat buying.

questions.stem: At a Vancouver mall pop-up, Alpine Audio invites passers-by to step into a soundproof booth, remix a track using its headphones, and post the result to the brand's social media challenge. Which advocacy funnel stage is Alpine targeting?
questions.explanation: Engagement invites potential customers to participate in the product experience and interact with its marketing: remixing in the booth and joining a branded challenge. Trial would mean obtaining a free sample or getting the product as a limited trial or download.

questions.stem: Zenith Meditation lets new users download its app and use every premium feature free for 14 days before any billing begins. Which stage of the customer advocacy funnel does this offer target?
questions.explanation: Trial is when customers obtain free samples or get the product as a limited trial or download. Purchase comes next, when positive experiences during the trial lead users to pay.

questions.stem: Nomad Coffee gives its longest-standing subscribers early access to rare roasts and a behind-the-scenes farm tour. Many then post glowing recommendations and refer friends. Which funnel stage do these actions reflect?
questions.explanation: In the advocacy stage, loyal customers are rewarded with additional experiences and become advocates who recommend the product to others. Loyalty is repeat purchasing; the recommending is what marks advocacy.

questions.stem: Trailhead Tents uses search engine optimization, online video, and display ads to drive people who have never heard of it to its website. Which advocacy funnel stage is this?
questions.explanation: The course's awareness example is a company using a website, SEO, online video, and display ads to drive consumers to an online destination. Interest comes after people know the brand, when attributes are highlighted so they want to learn more.

questions.stem: On its product page, KettleCraft highlights its kettle's 60-second boil time and stay-cool handle so curious visitors want to learn more. Which funnel stage is this designed for?
questions.explanation: Interest is the stage where interesting product attributes are highlighted to prompt potential customers to learn more. Engagement goes further, inviting people to participate in the product experience and interact with marketing.

questions.stem: After a two-week free trial, Mei enjoys Zest Meal Kits so much that she pays for her first full month of deliveries. Which advocacy funnel stage has Mei just reached?
questions.explanation: Purchase is the stage where positive product experiences (here, during the trial) lead to buying the product. Loyalty comes later, when ongoing positive experiences lead to repeat purchases over time.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly lists the LAST four stages of the customer advocacy funnel, in order?
questions.explanation: The full funnel is awareness, interest, engagement, trial, purchase, loyalty, advocacy. Trial comes before purchase, and loyalty (repeat purchase) comes before advocacy (recommending to others).

questions.stem: What distinguishes the loyalty stage from the advocacy stage of the customer advocacy funnel?
options: Loyalty is repeat purchasing driven by ongoing positive experiences; advocacy is loyal customers recommending the product to others
Loyalty is obtaining free samples or a limited trial; advocacy is making the first full-price purchase
Loyalty is recommending the product to friends and family; advocacy is buying the product again and again
Loyalty is the final stage of the funnel and comes after advocacy, once customers stop recommending
questions.explanation: Ongoing positive experiences lead to repeat purchases (loyalty), often encouraged by CRM programs; loyal customers who are rewarded with additional experiences then recommend the product (advocacy). Calling loyalty 'recommending to friends' and advocacy 'buying again and again' swaps the two definitions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a stage of the customer advocacy funnel?
questions.explanation: The funnel's seven stages are awareness, interest, engagement, trial, purchase, loyalty, and advocacy. Evaluation belongs to the hierarchy of effects (awareness, interest, evaluation, trial, adoption).

questions.stem: A Halifax skincare brand's online quiz and video tutorials attract many active participants, but analytics show few go on to buy because they're unsure the product suits their skin. According to the advocacy funnel, which tactic targets the NEXT stage?
options: Run more display ads to build awareness
Launch a points program that rewards repeat purchases
Offer free trial-size samples matched to quiz results
Give referral rewards to customers who recommend the brand
questions.explanation: Customers are already at engagement (participating and interacting), so the next stage is trial; free samples let them test the product before buying. A points program targets loyalty, which only makes sense after people have purchased.

questions.stem: Ginger Inc. is focusing its communication efforts to build awareness and create demand for its products amongst consumers. Ginger, Inc. is adopting a(n):
questions.explanation: A pull strategy focuses communication efforts on ultimate consumers to build awareness, trial, and demand, so consumers pull the product through the channel. A push strategy would aim the effort at distributors, wholesalers, and retailers instead.

questions.stem: A tech company develops a new smartphone and decides to promote it by offering incentives and training to mobile phone retailers and sales staff. This approach is designed to:
options: Focus communication efforts on ultimate consumers to build awareness, trial, and demand for a product
Influence the distribution channel to support and sell the product
Build a direct relationship with customers
questions.explanation: Incentives and training for retailers and their sales staff are a push strategy: communication aimed at the distribution channel to gain support through listings, sales, merchandising, feature pricing, and inclusion in flyers. Focusing on ultimate consumers to build awareness, trial, and demand describes a pull strategy, which targets consumers rather than the channel.

questions.stem: Harvest Gold Foods offers grocery chains a trade allowance, pays for end-aisle displays, and contributes co-op advertising funds so retailers feature its new soup in their weekly flyers. Harvest Gold is using:
questions.explanation: Trade allowances, merchandising (display) allowances, and co-op advertising funds are trade promotions directed at channel members, which is a push strategy. A pull strategy would aim advertising and consumer promotions at shoppers.

questions.stem: Lumen Skincare runs Instagram ads, mails free samples to consumers, and places its serum in a popular YouTube beauty series so shoppers start asking pharmacies to stock it. Lumen is using:
questions.explanation: Advertising, consumer promotion, and product placement aimed at end consumers create demand that pulls the product through the channel. A push strategy would target the pharmacies themselves with trade promotions and personal selling.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts push and pull strategies?
options: Push focuses on consumers, media, and the public; pull focuses on distributors, wholesalers, and retailers
Push focuses on distributors, wholesalers, and retailers; pull focuses on consumers, media, and the public
Push uses only advertising; pull uses only trade shows
Push and pull are two names for the same strategy
questions.explanation: Figure 12-2 shows push aimed at the channel (distributors, wholesalers, retailers) and pull aimed at consumers, media, and the public. Saying push focuses on consumers and pull on the channel reverses them, which is the most common trap.

questions.stem: A brand manager reports that her campaign won new listings at two national chains, better merchandising displays, feature pricing, and inclusion in retailer flyers. These results are associated with:
options: the advocacy stage of the funnel
questions.explanation: Figure 12-2 lists listings, sales, merchandising displays, feature pricing, and inclusion in flyers as the results sought by a push strategy. Pull results are consumer outcomes such as awareness, trial, loyalty, and advocacy.

questions.stem: According to Figure 12-2, which result is NOT typically sought by a pull strategy?
questions.explanation: Pull results are consumer outcomes: awareness, interest, recognition, trial, purchase, loyalty, and advocacy. Retailer listings are a push result, gained by influencing the channel.

questions.stem: Why does Figure 12-2 note that push and pull strategies should 'work together'?
options: Pull-created demand is wasted if stores don't stock the product, and push-won shelf space needs consumer demand to sell through
The Competition Act requires every manufacturer to run both strategies at once whenever it launches a product
Push and pull use exactly the same tools, so running both together adds almost nothing to the budget
A firm can use only one strategy per PLC stage, so it must alternate between push and pull each year
questions.explanation: Pull creates consumer demand and push secures distribution and in-store support; each is weaker without the other. The tools differ (trade promotions vs advertising and consumer promotion), so the claim that push and pull use exactly the same tools is wrong.

questions.stem: In Figure 12-2, personal selling appears as a tool for both push and pull strategies.
questions.explanation: True. Personal selling is listed in the push column (aimed at channel members) and in the pull column alongside advertising, publicity, consumer promotion, product placement, event marketing, and social media and sponsorship. So 'personal selling' alone doesn't tell you the strategy; look at who is being targeted.

questions.stem: Before launching a new advertising campaign, a company first defines what they hope to achieve, such as increasing brand awareness or boosting sales. This initial step in the marketing communications process is:
options: evaluating the program and recommending changes
scheduling and running the IMC elements
questions.explanation: Step 1 of the six-step process is specifying the IMC objectives: deciding what the program should achieve before anything else. Evaluating the program is the final step (6), when results are compared against those objectives.

questions.stem: Before writing any ads, Fjord Outdoor profiles the 25-to-40-year-old urban hikers it wants to reach: their lifestyle, media habits, and every place they encounter the brand. Which step of the marketing communications process is this?
options: Evaluating the program and recommending changes
questions.explanation: Step 2, identifying the target audience, means understanding who you're trying to reach (demographics, lifestyle, media habits) and considering their customer touch points. Designing the program (step 4) uses this knowledge to choose tools and messages.

questions.stem: Mosaic Mobile's team decides that its phone launch will combine TikTok videos, influencer partnerships, in-store displays, and a sampling event, and develops the creative message for each. Which step of the process is this?
options: Scheduling and running the IMC elements
questions.explanation: Choosing which promotional tools to use and developing their messages is designing the promotional program (step 4). Scheduling (step 5) comes after and decides when, how often, and how long each element runs.

questions.stem: A Saskatoon furniture retailer determines that it will spend $180,000 on promotion next year after costing out the tasks needed to reach its goals. Which step of the marketing communications process is this?
questions.explanation: Deciding how much to spend is step 3, setting the promotional budget, here using the objective-and-task method. Designing the program (step 4) then uses that budget to choose tools and messages.

questions.stem: Which step immediately precedes 'schedule and run the IMC elements' in the marketing communications process?
options: Evaluate the program and recommend changes
questions.explanation: Step 4, designing the promotional program, comes right before step 5, scheduling and running the elements: you must choose the tools before deciding their timing. Setting the budget is step 3.

questions.stem: In Figure 12-3, customer touch points and the product life cycle are flagged as considerations at which steps, respectively?
options: Step 4 (design the program) and step 2 (target audience)
Step 2 (target audience) and step 4 (design the program)
questions.explanation: Customer touch points are considered when identifying the target audience (step 2), and the product life cycle is considered when designing the promotional program (step 4). Pairing touch points with step 4 and the PLC with step 2 reverses them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the six steps in the marketing communications process?
options: Evaluate the program and recommend changes
questions.explanation: Selecting intermediaries is a distribution (place) decision. The six steps are specify objectives, identify the target audience, set the budget, design the program, schedule and run, and evaluate and recommend changes.

questions.stem: Marketer A is choosing between a continuous and a flighting schedule and fixing the exact weeks each video runs. Marketer B is choosing whether to use influencers or printed flyers to carry the message. Which steps are they in, respectively?
options: A: designing the promotional program; B: scheduling and running the IMC elements
A: setting the budget; B: identifying the target audience
A: evaluating the program; B: specifying the IMC objectives
A: scheduling and running the IMC elements; B: designing the promotional program
questions.explanation: Timing decisions (continuous vs flighting, which weeks) belong to step 5, scheduling and running; choosing which tools carry the message belongs to step 4, designing the program. Labelling A as designing the program and B as scheduling swaps the two.

questions.stem: Polaris Bank sets a goal to raise unaided awareness of its new no-fee student account from 10% to 30% among Calgary post-secondary students by spring. This is:
questions.explanation: Awareness is a communication objective, which builds the foundation for customer relationships. Being measurable (10% to 30%) doesn't make it behavioural; behavioural objectives involve actions such as trial or purchase.

questions.stem: Which option correctly classifies these two objectives? (1) Improve consumers' attitudes toward the brand. (2) Increase repeat purchases by 15%.
questions.explanation: Attitudes are a communication objective (laying the foundation for relationships); repeat purchase is an action-oriented behavioural objective. Calling attitudes behavioural and repeat purchases communication reverses them.

questions.stem: In the hierarchy of effects, which stage comes between interest and trial?
questions.explanation: The hierarchy of effects runs awareness, interest, evaluation, trial, adoption. Engagement sits between interest and trial in the customer advocacy funnel, a different model and a common mix-up.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a stage in the hierarchy of effects?
questions.explanation: The hierarchy of effects is awareness, interest, evaluation, trial, adoption. Loyalty is a stage of the customer advocacy funnel, not the hierarchy of effects.

questions.stem: Why does the course describe communication objectives as laying 'the foundation to build customer relationships'?
options: Because they are measured in dollars of revenue, which shows directly how much each relationship is worth
Because people generally need to know about and feel positively toward a brand before they try it and buy it
Because they replace behavioural objectives once sales begin, so the firm can stop tracking purchases
Because the Competition Act requires every campaign to state an awareness target before it runs
questions.explanation: Awareness, knowledge, and attitudes set up the later action-oriented outcomes (trial, purchase, repeat purchase), mirroring the hierarchy of effects. They don't replace behavioural objectives; firms typically set both.

questions.stem: All the points of contact between a customer and a brand (ads, packaging, the store, the website, service calls) are called:
questions.explanation: Customer touch points are every place a customer comes into contact with the brand, considered when identifying the target audience. Channels of distribution are the routes a product takes to market, not points of communication contact.

questions.stem: Brightline Optometry maps every place a patient encounters its brand: its Google listing, the booking app, the reminder text, the waiting room, the eyewear bag, and the follow-up survey. Brightline is identifying its:
questions.explanation: Listing every point of contact between customer and brand is mapping customer touch points, which supports step 2 (identify the target audience). A promotional schedule sets the timing and frequency of promotional tools, not points of contact.

questions.stem: Why should marketers consider customer touch points when identifying the target audience?
options: Touch points determine which stage of the product life cycle the product is currently in
Knowing where and how the audience encounters the brand shows which channels and moments can carry a consistent message
Touch points are the inputs needed to calculate a percentage-of-sales promotional budget
Advertising Standards Canada requires a complete touch-point map before any campaign can run
questions.explanation: Understanding the audience's points of contact reveals where messages will actually reach them and where consistency matters, which is central to IMC. The PLC is considered at step 4 and isn't determined by touch points.

questions.stem: IMC messages can be directed at consumers, intermediaries, or both. Which promotional program has a target audience of INTERMEDIARIES rather than consumers?
options: A paint maker's Instagram tutorials aimed at do-it-yourself homeowners
A paint maker's TV ads aimed at young families
A paint maker's trade-show booth and dealer incentives aimed at hardware-store owners
A paint maker's in-store coupons aimed at shoppers
questions.explanation: Hardware-store owners are channel members, so a trade show and dealer incentives target intermediaries. In-store coupons may be redeemed in the store, but they're aimed at shoppers, who are consumers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a customer touch point for a restaurant chain?
options: A server's greeting at the table
An internal spreadsheet of supplier costs
questions.explanation: Touch points are points of contact between the customer and the brand; the app, packaging, and service staff all shape customer impressions. An internal cost spreadsheet is never seen by customers, so it isn't a touch point.

questions.stem: Every year, Chinook Hardware sets its promotional budget at 4% of the previous year's sales. Which budgeting method is this?
questions.explanation: Setting the budget as a fixed percentage of past or anticipated sales is the percentage-of-sales method. Competitive parity would base the figure on what rivals spend.

questions.stem: After learning that its main rival spends about $2 million a year on advertising, Lakeshore Mattress sets its own budget at $2 million. Which method is Lakeshore using?
questions.explanation: Matching competitors' spending (or share of market) is competitive parity. Its weakness is that it ignores Lakeshore's own objectives, unlike objective and task.

questions.stem: The owner of a two-location bakery in Red Deer pays rent, wages, and suppliers first; whatever money is left at the end of the month goes to promotion. Which budgeting method is this?
questions.explanation: Funding promotion with money left after other budget items is the all-you-can-afford method, common in small businesses. It has no link to goals or to sales levels.

questions.stem: Aurora Fitness wants 3,000 new trial memberships. It lists the tasks needed (six weeks of social ads, a sampling event, and a direct-mail drop) and totals their costs to set its budget. Which method is this?
questions.explanation: Objective and task sets objectives, outlines the tasks required to meet them, and totals the cost. It's considered the best approach because spending is tied to what the firm wants to accomplish.

questions.stem: Last year Kestrel Outfitters had sales of $3,200,000. If it sets its promotional budget at 3.5% of last year's sales, how much will it budget for promotion?
questions.explanation: Percentage of sales: $3,200,000 x 0.035 = $112,000. $1,120,000 comes from multiplying by 0.35 (35%) and $11,200 from 0.0035 (0.35%), both decimal-place errors.

questions.stem: What is the main criticism of the percentage-of-sales budgeting method?
options: It treats sales as the cause of promotion rather than its result, so spending drops just when sales are weak
It copies competitors' spending levels and so ignores the firm's own objectives for the campaign
It can be used only by small firms that fund promotion from whatever cash is left over
It requires detailed judgment about the cost of every task needed to reach each objective
questions.explanation: Percentage of sales has backwards logic: sales determine promotion, when promotion is supposed to drive sales, so a sales slump automatically cuts the budget. Copying competitors is the flaw of competitive parity, and needing judgment about task costs is objective and task's drawback.

questions.stem: Which statement about promotional budgeting methods is NOT correct?
options: Objective and task starts with objectives and costs out the tasks needed to reach them
Competitive parity matches competitors' spending or share of market
Percentage of sales bases the budget on the firm's communication objectives
All-you-can-afford is common among small firms
questions.explanation: Percentage of sales bases the budget on past or anticipated sales, not on objectives; only objective and task starts from objectives. The other three statements are accurate descriptions.

questions.stem: The product life cycle is useful in describing the phases a product moves through from launch to discontinuation, but the PLC also helps marketers in:
options: choosing the appropriate communication tools at each phase of the cycle
creating the most effective messaging for the product
questions.explanation: All products have a life cycle, and the composition of the promotional mix changes from one phase to the next, which is why the PLC is considered at step 4, designing the promotional program. Budgeting is a separate step (3) using methods such as objective and task.

questions.stem: In the maturity stage of a popular line of kitchen appliances, the company's marketing objective is most likely to:
options: Increase consumer awareness of the product category
Persuade consumers to choose their brand over competitors
Maintain existing buyers with reminder advertising and sales promotions
Reduce promotional spending to maximize profits
questions.explanation: In maturity the goal is to maintain existing buyers: advertising reminds buyers of the product and sales promotions help maintain loyalty. Reducing promotional spending describes the decline stage (phase out), and persuading against competitors is the growth-stage objective.

questions.stem: Orbit Robotics has just launched Canada's first window-cleaning robot. It sends units to tech magazines for reviews, runs ads explaining what the product does, and has its salesforce call on electronics retailers. What is Orbit's promotional objective at this stage?
questions.explanation: Magazine publicity, explanatory advertising, and salesforce calls on intermediaries are introduction-stage activities, where the objective is to inform. Persuading comes in growth, once competitors arrive.

questions.stem: Two years later, several rivals sell robot window cleaners. Orbit's ads now stress why its model cleans faster than competing brands, and its reps work hard to keep intermediaries carrying it. What is Orbit's promotional objective now?
questions.explanation: In growth, personal selling to intermediaries and advertising that differentiates the product from competing brands serve the objective to persuade. Reminding is the maturity-stage objective, after the market has settled.

questions.stem: Sales of Vista Electronics' DVD players have dwindled, and the company plans to discontinue them soon. It now spends very little money on promoting them. What is its promotional objective?
questions.explanation: Little money spent on promotion is the decline-stage activity, where the objective is to phase out. Reminder advertising belongs to maturity, when the firm is still actively maintaining buyers.

questions.stem: According to Figure 12-4, which activity is NOT associated with the introduction stage?
options: Sales promotion in the form of free samples
questions.explanation: Introduction activities are publicity in magazines, advertising, the salesforce calling on intermediaries, and free samples. Reminder advertising is a maturity-stage activity, when the goal is to remind.

questions.stem: Figure 12-4 uses sales promotion in two different stages. Which pairing is correct?
options: Introduction: discounts and coupons; maturity: free samples
Growth: free samples; decline: discounts and coupons
Introduction: free samples; maturity: discounts, coupons, and events
questions.explanation: Free samples help new buyers try a product in introduction; discounts, coupons, and events help keep existing buyers in maturity. Pairing discounts and coupons with introduction and free samples with maturity reverses the two stages.

questions.stem: Amy is in the midst of deciding on specific timing of TV advertisements and online video placements. She is most likely engaged in:
questions.explanation: The promotional schedule describes when each promotional tool is used and for what frequency and duration, so deciding the timing of TV ads and video placements is scheduling (step 5). Designing the program (step 4) decides which tools and messages to use, not when they run.

questions.stem: A Banff ski resort advertises heavily from October to February and runs no advertising at all from March to September. Which scheduling approach is this?
questions.explanation: Flighting alternates periods of advertising with periods of no advertising. Pulse would keep a steady base of advertising all year and add bursts at peak times, but the resort goes completely dark.

questions.stem: A national grocery chain runs a steady base of weekly flyers all year, then adds bursts of heavy TV advertising before Thanksgiving, Christmas, and back-to-school. Which scheduling approach is this?
questions.explanation: Pulse scheduling combines a continuous base level of promotion with periodic bursts. It isn't flighting, because flighting includes periods with no activity at all.

questions.stem: What is the difference between flighting and pulse schedules?
options: Flighting keeps a continuous base with periodic bursts; pulse alternates periods of activity with none
Flighting alternates periods of activity with periods of none; pulse keeps a continuous base with periodic bursts
Flighting is used for push strategies; pulse is used for pull strategies
Flighting runs at the same level every week; pulse runs only once a year
questions.explanation: In flighting, advertising stops completely between flights; in pulse, there is always a base level of activity, with spikes at key times. Describing flighting as a continuous base with bursts and pulse as on-and-off periods swaps the two definitions.

questions.stem: In the marketing communications process, the promotional schedule describes:
options: the percentage of last year's sales assigned to each promotional tool in the budget
the stages a customer moves through, from first awareness of the brand to advocacy
the order in which each promotional tool is introduced and the frequency and duration of its use
the regulatory approvals that ASC and the CRTC require before a campaign can run
questions.explanation: The promotional schedule sets the order, frequency, and duration of each tool, as part of step 5, scheduling and running the IMC elements. The stages from awareness to advocacy describe the customer advocacy funnel.

questions.stem: Frostline Tire sells winter tires that Canadians buy almost entirely in October and November. Which scheduling approach fits best?
questions.explanation: When demand is concentrated in a short season, flighting puts spending into that window and goes dark the rest of the year. Continuous scheduling would waste money advertising steadily when almost no one is buying.

questions.stem: Following the completion of a marketing campaign, a company reviews metrics such as sales data, customer feedback, and digital engagement to understand the effectiveness of the campaign and areas for improvement. This final step in the marketing communications process is:
options: evaluating the program and recommending changes
scheduling and running the IMC elements
questions.explanation: Step 6, evaluating the program and recommending changes, compares results such as sales, feedback, and engagement with the objectives and identifies improvements. Specifying objectives is step 1, which sets the targets this evaluation measures against.

questions.stem: Halcyon Tea shows two versions of a new commercial to a consumer panel to choose which one to air. After the campaign runs, it surveys viewers to measure recall. These two research activities are, respectively:
options: a communication objective and a behavioural objective
questions.explanation: Pretests evaluate promotional elements before they run (choosing between ad versions); posttests evaluate them after (measuring recall). Calling the panel test a posttest and the recall survey a pretest reverses the order.

questions.stem: Halo Fitness tracks click-through rates, conversion rates, and engagement rates on its campaign posts to judge how well the campaign is working. These measures are examples of:
options: digital engagement metrics used in program evaluation
customer touch points mapped when identifying the audience
barriers to effective communication with the audience
results sought by a push strategy aimed at retailers
questions.explanation: Click-throughs, conversions, and engagement rates are digital metrics used in step 6 to evaluate the program. Push results are trade outcomes such as listings and displays, not consumer engagement measures.

questions.stem: Which activity is NOT part of the 'evaluate the program and recommend changes' step?
options: Comparing campaign sales results with the objectives
Running posttests to measure ad recall
Deciding which weeks the TV ads will air
Reviewing customer feedback and engagement rates
questions.explanation: Deciding when ads air is scheduling (step 5). Comparing results with objectives, posttesting, and reviewing feedback and engagement all belong to evaluation (step 6).

questions.stem: Prairie Cycle's posttest shows strong ad recall, meeting its communication objective, but trial purchases are far below its behavioural objective. What should the team recommend?
options: Declare the campaign a success, because high ad recall shows the program fully worked
Cut nearly all promotion, since weak trial means the product must be in decline
Switch to the competitive-parity method so the budget simply matches rivals' spending
Revise the program, for example by adding trial-driving tools such as samples or a limited-time offer
questions.explanation: Evaluation exists to recommend changes; awareness without action calls for tools that move people to trial, such as sales promotion. Declaring success ignores the unmet behavioural objective, and cutting promotion is a decline-stage response with no evidence of decline.

questions.stem: Loft & Grain, a Halifax furniture maker, publishes room-design guides, ranks near the top of Google for 'small apartment storage ideas,' and posts how-to videos so buyers find it while searching. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Inbound communications require excellent content and the ability to be seen in the right places, so customers come to the brand. Outbound would send messages out through ads, cold calls, or direct mail.

questions.stem: Granite Roofing buys radio spots, cold-calls homeowners, and mails flyers to every house in a northwest Calgary neighbourhood. This approach is:
questions.explanation: Advertising, cold calls, and direct mail sent out to audiences are traditional outbound communications. Inbound relies on content that customers find on their own.

questions.stem: According to the course, why can inbound communications be considerably more cost-effective than outbound?
options: Because interested consumers find the content themselves, so the firm isn't paying to push messages at audiences who may not care
Because inbound content never requires any investment in writing, video, design, or search optimization
Because the CRTC subsidizes Canadian content marketing that appears in search results and on social media
Because inbound is funded by trade allowances that retailers pay manufacturers for featured placement
questions.explanation: Inbound requires excellent content and visibility in the right places; when people who are already interested come to you, spending isn't wasted on broad outbound reach. It still requires investment in content (writing, video, search optimization), so the claim that inbound needs no investment is wrong.

questions.stem: A soft-drink brand runs national TV commercials aimed at consumers to build demand. How is this best classified?
options: Inbound communication supporting a push strategy
Inbound communication supporting a pull strategy
Outbound communication supporting a push strategy
Outbound communication supporting a pull strategy
questions.explanation: TV advertising is traditional outbound communication, and because it targets consumers to create demand it supports a pull strategy. Inbound and pull are not synonyms: inbound describes customers finding the brand, while pull describes who the communication targets.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of inbound communication?
options: Search-optimized blog posts answering common customer questions
A telemarketing campaign calling numbers from a purchased list
A how-to YouTube series that people find through search
A free downloadable guide promoted through the brand's social profiles
questions.explanation: Telemarketing sends messages out to people who didn't seek them, which is outbound. Search-optimized posts, findable tutorials, and downloadable guides all draw interested customers in.

questions.stem: A brand regularly updates its official blog and social media profiles with new content about its products and services. This approach to marketing primarily uses:
questions.explanation: Owned media refers to the channels a company controls, at least in part, typically its website, blog, and social media profiles. Earned media would be coverage or reviews created by others, such as journalists and customers.

questions.stem: Willow Bakery's sourdough has collected dozens of five-star Google and Yelp reviews written by customers. In the digital channels framework, these reviews are:
questions.explanation: Review websites such as Yelp and Amazon reviews are earned media, generated by others rather than paid for or controlled by the bakery. Owned media would be Willow's own website or social pages.

questions.stem: Velo Coffee pays three Toronto lifestyle creators to post about its new cold brew, and separately sends a weekly promotional email to its subscriber list. Using the course's digital channels slide, how should both activities be classified?
questions.explanation: The Keller/Swaminathan slide lists both paid bloggers/influencers and e-mail marketing under paid media. The tempting answer calls email owned because the subscriber list belongs to the company, but the course classifies e-mail marketing as paid.

questions.stem: Which set contains ONLY owned media?
options: Company website, Yelp reviews, mobile app
Company Facebook page, Facebook ads, company website
Company website, company YouTube channel, mobile app
Mobile app, mobile in-app ads, company blog
questions.explanation: Websites, company-owned social channels such as a YouTube channel, and mobile apps are owned media. Facebook ads and in-app ads are paid, and Yelp reviews are earned, which rules out the other sets.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of paid media?
options: Media coverage of a product launch
questions.explanation: Media coverage is earned media, because journalists choose to cover the brand. Search, display, and mobile in-app advertising all appear under paid media on the course slide.

questions.stem: Exposure generated by others (such as customer reviews, public relations, and media coverage) that the company neither buys nor controls is called:
questions.explanation: Earned media comes from third parties such as customers and journalists. Owned media is controlled by the company (its website, social pages, apps), and paid media is bought.

questions.stem: A new Calgary kombucha brand has no budget for advertising but wants a channel it fully controls, where it can tell its story and take orders. What should it build first?
options: A campaign of Google search ads
A set of paid influencer partnerships
A strategy for collecting Yelp reviews
Its own website and mobile-friendly online store
questions.explanation: A company website is owned media: the firm controls it and doesn't have to buy ad space. Search ads and paid influencers are paid media, and reviews are earned media the brand can't control.

questions.stem: A Calgary radio station now streams its morning show live online and releases each segment as a podcast. Which trend in the changing communications landscape does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: The course's evolving media list includes radio stations streaming content and creating podcasts. Connected consumers refers to consumers' access to fast, affordable Internet services and devices, not to how media outlets change.

questions.stem: The trend in which affordable and fast Internet technology provides consumers with easy-to-use services and devices that facilitate marketing communications is called:
questions.explanation: That is the course's definition of connected consumers. Evolving media describes changes in media outlets and formats, such as streaming-only content and digital boards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed in the course as an example of evolving media?
options: Out-of-home advertising being replaced with digital boards
News organizations moving content back to print-only editions
questions.explanation: Every evolving-media example moves toward digital: streaming-only content, traditional media building online assets, news on YouTube and apps, radio streaming and podcasts, digital boards, and mobile ads. News organizations actually deliver content through YouTube channels and apps, not by returning to print only.

questions.stem: According to the course, why are traditional media outlets such as TV networks and newspapers creating their own online assets?
options: To remain competitive and relevant as audiences shift online
To comply with CRTC rules that ban print and broadcast advertising
To reduce the number of connected consumers
To replace the need for measurement companies
questions.explanation: The evolving media slide says traditional media are creating their own online assets to remain competitive and relevant. There is no rule banning print or broadcast; the shift is driven by audience behaviour.

questions.stem: Which scenario illustrates connected consumers rather than evolving media?
options: A TV network launches a new drama series produced strictly for streaming on its own app
A national newspaper starts delivering its daily stories through a YouTube channel and a news app
A downtown billboard owner replaces printed posters with a digital screen that rotates several ads
A shopper in a store uses her phone to compare prices, read reviews, and watch a product demo
questions.explanation: Connected consumers is about consumers using affordable, fast Internet services and devices, like a smartphone in a store. The other three describe media outlets and formats changing, which is evolving media.

questions.stem: Instead of listing policy features, Northern Hearth Insurance releases a short film that follows a Fort McMurray family rebuilding their home after a wildfire, with their agent helping at every step. Northern Hearth is using:
questions.explanation: Storytelling builds relationships by conveying events with images and words, engaging people through emotions and experiences. It isn't product placement, because this is the brand's own narrative, not a paid appearance in someone else's entertainment content.

questions.stem: According to the course, storytelling builds relationships by conveying events using _____ and words.
questions.explanation: Storytelling conveys events using images and words, and stories engage people through emotions and experiences. Statistics and prices belong to feature-and-price messaging, which storytelling deliberately moves away from.

questions.stem: According to the course, why is storytelling an effective marketing communications approach?
options: Stories pack in more technical specifications and product detail than any other message format
Stories engage people through their emotions and experiences, motivating them to act and to more readily accept an idea
Stories are exempt from the Canadian Code of Advertising Standards, so their claims face no review
Stories guarantee earned media coverage because journalists are expected to report on brand narratives
questions.explanation: The course says stories engage people through emotions and experiences, which motivates them to act and to more readily accept a concept or idea. Storytelling is not exempt from advertising standards; ASC's Code applies to advertising generally.

questions.stem: Which campaign uses storytelling rather than conventional feature-based advertising?
options: A lotion ad that lists its seven active ingredients, its SPF rating, and its dermatologist approval
A banner ad that reads 'Now 30% more moisturizing than our original formula' beside the bottle
A flyer offering 20% off all body care products this weekend only at every store location
A video following a real woman's journey to self-confidence, inviting viewers to rethink beauty
questions.explanation: A narrative about a real person's experience that engages emotions is storytelling, like the course's Dove example. Ingredient lists and claims are feature-based advertising, and a weekend discount is sales promotion.

questions.stem: A Saskatoon animal shelter's flyers listing adoption fees and opening hours aren't increasing adoptions. Applying the course's view of storytelling, what should the shelter do?
options: Share the story of one rescued dog's journey from intake to a new family, using photos and video
Add more statistics about shelter capacity and intake numbers to the existing flyer
Offer a coupon for half-price adoption fees to anyone who visits this month
Print twice as many flyers and distribute them more often around the city
questions.explanation: Storytelling uses images and words to engage emotions and experiences, motivating action, and one dog's journey does that far better than facts. A fee coupon is sales promotion, which may spark short-term action but isn't storytelling.

questions.stem: Prairie Harvest Foods hires TrueNorth Collective to handle its market research, creative development, media planning and buying, and ad production. TrueNorth is a:
questions.explanation: A full-service agency offers the complete range of services: research, creative, media, and production. A creative boutique is a limited-service agency that handles only the creative work.

questions.stem: Coastline Telecom set up its own internal department that writes, designs, and places all of its advertising instead of hiring an outside firm. This department is a(n):
questions.explanation: An in-house agency is an advertising department within the advertiser's own company. A full-service agency is an outside firm offering all services to many clients.

questions.stem: According to the course, the areas of the marketing communications industry work together to form an industry that is:
questions.explanation: The slide states that the industry's areas work together to form an industry that is ethical, trustworthy, cohesive, and measurable. Regulators and measurement companies are part of the industry precisely so it is not unregulated or unmeasured.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the areas that make up the marketing communications industry?
options: Regulators such as ASC and the CRTC
questions.explanation: The industry consists of advertisers, agencies, media, suppliers, regulators, and measurement companies. Wholesalers are marketing channel intermediaries that move products, not part of the communications industry.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a full-service agency from a limited-service agency?
options: A full-service agency is a department inside the advertiser's own company; a limited-service agency is an independent outside firm
A full-service agency offers research, creative, media, and production; a limited-service agency specializes in one area, such as creative or media buying
A full-service agency only plans and buys media; a limited-service agency only measures audiences and campaign results
A full-service agency regulates advertising content for the industry; a limited-service agency creates the ads themselves
questions.explanation: Full-service agencies provide the whole package, while limited-service (specialty) agencies such as creative boutiques or media-buying services focus on one function. Working inside the advertiser's company describes an in-house agency.

questions.stem: A consumer thinks a TV ad for a skin cream exaggerates its results and files a complaint under the Canadian Code of Advertising Standards. Which body administers this code?
questions.explanation: ASC is the advertising industry's self-regulatory body and administers the Canadian Code of Advertising Standards, including consumer complaints. The Competition Bureau enforces the federal Competition Act, a law rather than an industry code.

questions.stem: An Ontario electronics retailer advertises a TV as 'Regular $899, now $399' even though it never sold at $899. Which body enforces the federal law that prohibits this kind of misleading advertising?
questions.explanation: The Competition Bureau enforces the Competition Act, which prohibits misleading advertising and deceptive marketing practices such as inflated 'regular' prices. ASC handles ad complaints under the voluntary industry Code, not federal law.

questions.stem: A company wants to launch a new Canadian specialty TV channel and must obtain a broadcasting licence. Which body on the course's regulator list will it deal with?
questions.explanation: The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) regulates broadcasting and telecommunications, and also enforces Canada's anti-spam legislation. The CWTA is an industry association for wireless companies, not the broadcasting regulator.

questions.stem: The Canadian Marketing Association (CMA) is best described as:
options: the federal agency that enforces the Competition Act
the regulator that licenses broadcasters and enforces anti-spam rules
the national association of marketers, which sets a code of ethics and standards of practice
the self-regulatory body that administers the Canadian Code of Advertising Standards
questions.explanation: The CMA is the marketing profession's association, known for its code of ethics and standards of practice. The self-regulatory body that administers the Code of Advertising Standards is ASC.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between Advertising Standards Canada (ASC) and the Competition Bureau?
options: ASC is the industry's self-regulatory body administering the Code of Advertising Standards; the Competition Bureau is a federal agency enforcing the Competition Act
ASC enforces the federal Competition Act; the Competition Bureau administers the industry's Canadian Code of Advertising Standards
ASC regulates broadcasting licences and anti-spam rules; the Competition Bureau represents Canada's wireless carriers
ASC handles only mobile marketing complaints; the Competition Bureau handles only misleading claims in print advertising
questions.explanation: ASC is voluntary industry self-regulation through its Code, while the Competition Bureau enforces federal law against misleading advertising and deceptive marketing. Saying ASC enforces the Competition Act while the Competition Bureau administers the Code swaps their roles.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the six regulatory bodies listed on the course slide?
questions.explanation: The six bodies are ASC, the Competition Bureau, the CRTC, the CMA, the CWTA, and the MMA. The Better Business Bureau is not on the course's list.

questions.stem: A Montreal retailer plans a campaign in which shoppers text a keyword to a five-digit short code to join a VIP list. Which two bodies on the course list focus specifically on the wireless and mobile marketing space?
questions.explanation: The Canadian Wireless Telecommunications Association represents the wireless industry (including guidelines for text-message short codes), and the Mobile Marketing Association sets mobile marketing guidelines. The CRTC regulates broadcasting and telecom broadly, and ASC covers advertising in general.

questions.stem: Before launching its 'Fresh in 60 seconds' campaign, Prairie Burger trains every crew member on the promise, shows staff the ads before customers see them, and rewards teams that deliver. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Internal marketing treats the company's own employees as an audience so they can deliver the brand promise. A push strategy aims incentives and training at channel members such as independent retailers, not the firm's own crew.

questions.stem: A Calgary software company hires someone to shape how current and prospective employees see the firm as a place to work, including running its careers social accounts and employee-story videos. This emerging role is the:
questions.explanation: The course identifies the employer brand manager as an emerging role that manages the organization's image as an employer. A product manager manages a product brand's marketing, not the company's reputation with employees.

questions.stem: Why does the course describe internal marketing as a key to competitive advantage?
options: Because employees deliver the brand experience, so informed, engaged people make the external promise real
Because internal communications to staff are exempt from all Canadian advertising regulation
Because it removes the need to spend money on external IMC programs
Because employees count as earned media in the paid, owned, and earned framework
questions.explanation: The course stresses people as the source of competitive advantage: staff who understand and believe in the brand deliver the experience customers were promised. Internal marketing supports external IMC; it doesn't replace it.

questions.stem: Internal marketing and a push strategy can both involve training and incentives. What distinguishes them?
options: Internal marketing targets channel members such as retailers; push targets the firm's own employees and managers
Internal marketing targets the firm's own employees; push targets channel members such as retailers and wholesalers
Internal marketing is used only in the decline stage; push is used only in the introduction stage of the PLC
Internal marketing is a form of earned media; push is a form of owned media that the firm controls
questions.explanation: The audience decides it: internal marketing is aimed inside the organization at its own people, while push is aimed at intermediaries and their sales staff. Saying internal marketing targets channel members and push targets employees reverses the two audiences.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the course's points about internal marketing?
options: Internal marketing is a key to competitive advantage through people
The employer brand manager is an emerging role in organizations
Social media is important for employee engagement and content development
Internal marketing replaces the need for external marketing communications
questions.explanation: The course notes internal marketing's role in competitive advantage, the emerging employer brand manager role, and social media's importance for engagement and content (with the ultimate goal of creating experiences). Nothing says it replaces external communications; it supports them.
